description:
We are a group formed by 4 amazing Spanish space engineers willing to solve this challenge in the most creative and efficient way possible.

Sign up if you think you can fit in!!!
summary:
Near the Moon's south pole the Sun stays low on the horizon all year. Move a lander a few kilometres, or land a few days later, and it can lose its power or its line of sight to Earth. We built Lunar Site Evaluator so you can check that before committing to a site.

Pick a site and a date and the app shows, hour by hour through 2027, when that spot gets sunlight and when Earth is above the horizon, and how long until the next sunset or Earthset. You can filter 59 candidate sites by your own mission requirements on a 3D Moon, put two or three next to each other, look around from the surface in Street View, or play a short mission where your landing site falls through and you have to choose another.

It's aimed at the situation the challenge describes: a launch slips and someone has to re-check sites and dates fast. The Sun and Earth positions come from NASA's SPICE ephemerides, and we checked them against JPL Horizons; they agree to within 0.0007 degrees. The default view uses plain language so a student can follow along, and Pro mode shows the full technical detail.
details:
What it does:

The two things that decide a south pole landing are power and communications. Solar panels need the Sun above the local hills, and talking to Earth directly needs Earth above them too. Near the pole both come and go, and a site that looks great on day 1 can be dark and out of contact by day 9.

Lunar Site Evaluator puts 59 candidate landing sites, taken from published studies, on a 3D Moon and a polar map. You set what your mission needs, for example a minimum share of sunlight or of Earth visibility during your landing window, and the list of matching sites updates as you type. Each site shows how much of the time it is sunlit, how often Earth is in view, its longest dark stretch, its slope and how far it is from the nearest permanently shadowed crater. Site Check runs the same numbers for any latitude and longitude you enter.

Press Play on the mission clock and time runs through 2027 an hour at a time, with a countdown to the next sunset and Earthset. Compare puts two or three sites side by side and lines up their sunlight and Earth windows on one timeline, which is the quickest way to answer "if we slip a week, where should we go instead?". Street View drops you onto a site to see the terrain and where the Sun and Earth are in the sky. There is also a short mission game: your planned site falls through, you pick another, and the game tells you why it worked or why you ran out of light. The globe also shows 25 past landings for context.

How it works:

Everything heavy runs ahead of time in Python and is published as static files, so the website stays fast and doesn't need a server.

We compute the direction of the Sun and of Earth from the Moon for every hour of 2027 with NASA/NAIF SPICE (the DE440 ephemeris and the lunar orientation kernels), so libration is included. To make sure we weren't fooling ourselves, we asked the JPL Horizons API for the same angles at seven sites, including Apollo 11 and Chang'e 4. The biggest difference we found was 0.0007 degrees.

Terrain comes from NASA's LOLA elevation models: the south and north polar products from NASA PGDA and the global LDEM_64. We use them for relief, slopes, permanently shadowed regions and the local horizon in the 3D views. Each site then gets its metrics and a weighted score, and the same scoring code runs in the browser, which is why the filters react instantly. The site itself is React and TypeScript, with three.js for the globe and CesiumJS for Street View.

Who it's for:

Mission planners get a quick way to re-check sites and dates when plans change. Teachers and students get the same data in plain language, plus a game that shows why a few kilometres matter. Every site lists where its coordinates came from, and anyone can rerun our pipeline from open NASA data.

What we think is new:

The same clock drives everything on the page: the globe, the site numbers, the comparison and Street View. Change the date and you see the consequences everywhere at once. The app also works in both directions, from requirements to sites in Explore and from a chosen site to what happens next in the game. We tried hard to explain results rather than only rank them.

What we had to think about:

The Moon has no atmosphere, so there is no refraction to correct for. The horizon is the terrain plus the curvature of the Moon. Libration makes Earth wander around in the lunar sky, which matters a lot near the pole.

We also want to be upfront about the limits. The site sunlight and Earth figures currently assume a smooth horizon with a small margin for the antenna. Terrain horizons are computed for polar sites in the 3D views but are not yet part of every score, and a few map overlays are still placeholders.

Tools:

TypeScript, Python, HTML and CSS. React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, React Router, three.js with React Three Fiber, and CesiumJS on the web side. SpiceyPy, NumPy and the JPL Horizons API for the science. Vitest, pytest, ESLint, Prettier, Ruff and GitHub Actions for testing. Hosted on Vercel, code on GitHub, built on our own laptops.
